title: Coherent interaction of WS$_2$ and quasi-2D perovskite excitons over micrometer distances via a cavity field
authors: Marti Struve, Hamid Pashaei Adl, Jamie M. Fitzgerald, Oliwia Janikowska, Maciej Śmiertka, Alessandro Surrente, Sven Stephan, Christoph Lienau, Falk Eilenberger, Zdeněk Sofer, Watcharaphol Paritmongkol, William A. Tisdale, Paulina Plochocka, Ermin Malic, Christian Schneider, Martin Esmann
abstract: The coherent coupling of cavity-confined photons and excitonic matter resonances leads to the formation of cavity polaritons, hybrid light-matter quasi-particles. If multiple exciton resonances couple to the same photonic mode, the resulting polariton constitutes a coherent interaction between matter resonances that can be spatially separated without any direct electronic coupling. In this work, we demonstrate the formation of such a coherent coupling at room temperature using an open optical cavity containing two distinct van der Waals materials - monolayer WS2 and layered quasi-2D halide perovskites (HaPs) - separated by $1.5 μ\rm m$. The system forms three polariton branches, with the middle branch possessing nearly equal fractions of both excitons and the photonic mode. White-light reflectivity and luminescence measurements are in good agreement with simulations using a coupled harmonic oscillator and a microscopic Wannier-Hopfield framework. Our results lay the foundation to combine highly complementary degrees of freedom in 2D materials in an in-situ tunable fashion to enable new polaritonic functionalities.
summary: This paper reports on the coherent coupling of excitons from $	ext{WS}_2$ and quasi-2D perovskites mediated by a cavity photon mode across a micrometer gap. By combining advanced optical measurements with coupled oscillator theory, the authors confirm the formation of hybrid polaritons. This work establishes a platform for engineering novel light-matter functionalities in 2D materials.
main_problem: The research aims to demonstrate and characterize the coherent coupling between excitons from two distinct, spatially separated 2D materials ($	ext{WS}_2$ and quasi-2D perovskites) mediated by a single cavity photon mode.
main_result: The study successfully demonstrated the formation of three polariton branches, confirming coherent, photon-mediated interaction between the two excitonic systems over a micrometer separation distance.
method: The work combines experimental measurements (white-light reflectivity and photoluminescence) with theoretical modeling using coupled harmonic oscillator and Wannier-Hopfield frameworks.
model_or_system: The physical system is a hybrid heterostructure comprising a $	ext{WS}_2$ monolayer and a quasi-2D halide perovskite ($	ext{HaP}$) placed within an open optical microcavity. The system dynamics are modeled using coupled oscillator Hamiltonians.
key_observables: Polariton energy branches, coupling strengths ($g$), Hopfield coefficients, white-light reflectivity spectra, and photoluminescence (PL) intensity.
important_parameters: Separation distance ($\sim 1.5 \ \mu	ext{m}$), coupling strengths ($g_{	ext{WS}_2} \approx 16-20 	ext{ meV}$, $g_{	ext{HaP}} \approx 36 	ext{ meV}$), and cavity detuning.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on treating the system as a coupled set of harmonic oscillators and utilizes approximations like the Born-Markov approximation for scattering rates.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the physical setup involving DBR mirrors and transferred 2D materials, showing cavity tuning series data for the hybridized polariton and PL spectra for pure and mixed systems.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical setup and initial single-material coupling confirmations to analyzing the coupled three-oscillator Hamiltonian, and finally detailing the measurement of tunable polariton characteristics and scattering rates.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to AMO physics and quantum optics as it explores engineered light-matter interactions (polaritons) in solid-state systems, demonstrating coherent coupling over distances that typically suppress such interactions.
